Precious Metals Quarterly 2010 Q3 # Executive summary ## Silver: high prices to feed fundamental surplus Investors are continuing to be willing buyers and they have recently bid silver’s price up to a 30-year high. It is clear that even the market’s current fundamental excess of over 5,000 t/y is not sufficient to meet all of investors’ latent demand. In the meantime, main-product miners are continuing to line up their projects, which obviously appear to be attractive assets at present. - Fabrication demand has recovered strongly following a sharp fall in 2009 as a result of the contraction in industrial activity associated with the global financial crisis. - We expect silver’s price to peak by 2012, and a subsequent decline should curtail further main-product mine development, but not to the extent that output falls significantly. - Even with silver trading at around $10/oz, the market is still likely to be generating a fundamental surplus through to 2015 at which point stocks will have lifted during an eightyear period by the equivalent of one year’s fabrication demand. ### **Silver has recently reached a 30-year high** 24 London silver fix; $/oz

CRU International Limited confidential 2 Precious Metals Quarterly 2010 Q3 Executive Summary ## Other precious metal markets #### Gold After jumping almost 3½-fold last year, gold’s fundamental surplus is still set to widen further in 2011-15 as mine production at last reacts to higher prices and these same quotations put a cap on jewellery demand. So far, this has not undermined gold prices as investment purchases have stayed strong. However, at some point, worries about the economy will lessen and these flows will start to be redirected elsewhere. Even if existing holders of gold do not choose to cash in their investment, we therefore still expect gold’s bull run to end in the second half of next year. - Although concerns over the southern European economies have diminished somewhat of late, they have been replaced by more general worries that the major Western economies could be heading for a double-dip recession. - Net official coin sales have increased while ETF buying has remained strong. - The rebound in electronics demand has so far exceeded our expectations in 2010, but this has been offset by a new downward trend in jewellery fabrication since 2009 Q4. #### Platinum Although platinum’s market deficit is narrowing, it remains large enough for prices to come under pressure in the absence of investor demand. And, in contrast to gold, fears of a doubledip recession have undermined confidence in fabrication offtake more than they have boosted safe-haven investment. Thus, platinum prices have traded broadly sideways for the last three months, although

$1,500/oz is still seen as a buying opportunity, particularly in China. - Car production bounced strongly in the first quarter but has been falling back since April. The one saving grace is that a higher proportion of European sales are again diesel. - South African mine production has underperformed in aggregate too. - With both supply and demand lower, our latest market forecast is thus similar to last time, although higher electricity prices in South Africa will raise platinum’s cost floor. #### Palladium Even before investment buying, the palladium market may now be in deficit and, although surpluses could return in 2011-12, supply will again struggle to match demand after that. - Palladium demand in autocatalysts should be holding up better than that of platinum as the global share of markets with higher palladium loadings grows this year and into the future. - Stillwater has trimmed its guidance for 2010 production. - The successful launch of ETF Securities’ US contract has kept US metal from the market, and prices have risen as fabricators call on more of the palladium previously held in Swiss vaults. ## Data sources and study team 

The historical data presented in this report are based on estimates published by a variety of sources, including Johnson Matthey (JM), World Gold Council (WGC), International Financial Statistics (IFS), JD Power, London Bullion Market Association (LBMA), World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS), GTIS trade statistics, and company websites and written reports. 

However, CRU’s interpretation of these data may or may not coincide with those expressed in these various sources. 

The forecast is exclusively CRU’s. 

##### **This report is based on information available to CRU up until 24**<sup>**th**</sup> **September 2010.**
